To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the generalization of deep metric learning models is not only influenced by the distribution shift between training and test data, but also by the distribution shifts that occur within the training set.

1) The current evaluation of DML is too simplistic, 2) The performance under distribution shift is not well correlated with the performance on a fixed test set, and 3) We propose a novel evaluation protocol that considers a broad spectrum of data distributions, and show that the proposed evaluation protocol is more challenging and better aligned with real-world applications.
1) The performance of DML methods is strongly dependent on the distribution shift between train and test data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
three questions: (1) How can we characterize generalization in deep metric learning under distribution shifts?
the following questions: (i) How do different distribution shifts affect the performance of DML? (ii) What are the most challenging shifts for DML?
the following questions: 1) Can we quantify the degree of shift between training and test distributions?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current evaluation protocols are too narrow to provide a reliable measure of generalization.

(1) the current evaluation protocol is not sufficient to characterize generalization under OOD shift in deep metric learning, and (2) there is no clear evidence of a generalization gap in the considered setting.
DML is not a robust approach, as the performance is very dependent on the data split and distribution shift.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a new benchmark and a new metric for the evaluation of DML methods.

1) we show that the current DML benchmarks are not suitable for evaluating generalization under out-of-distribution shifts, 2) we introduce the Out-Of-Domain Generalization Benchmark (OODGB), a new benchmark that includes a broad range of distribution shifts with varying degrees of difficulty, 3) we show that current DML methods fail to generalize to out-of-distribution data.
we propose a novel benchmark for DML that includes a wide range of data distribution shifts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DML algorithms are surprisingly resilient to distribution shift, and that their generalization ability can be characterized by the number of classes in the train and test sets.
the performance of DML methods is not as robust as it may seem at first sight.
DML generalizes well to out-of-distribution data.
